# Proposal {#sec-proposal}

## Title

Affordable Housing in Albany, New York

## Literature Review

Housing affordability is commonly measured by comparing housing costs with household income[@hudAffordableHousing]. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) generally considers housing affordable when housing costs are no more than 30 percent of household income. Households that spend more than this amount may have less money available for other important needs. This project uses rent and income data to examine differences in housing affordability across census tracts in Albany, New York.

## Project Description

### Research Question

How does housing affordability vary across census tracts in Albany, New York?

### Why This Matters

Housing affordability is an important issue because housing costs can affect where people are able to live. This project will help show how housing affordability differs across areas of Albany, New York.

## Data

This project uses three data sets from the U.S. Census Bureau, all for census tracts in Albany, New York:

- **Median gross rent** — 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-Year Estimates, table B25064. Source: data.census.gov. License: U.S. government work, (not under copyright in the United States). Accessed 2026-09-21. 87 rows (consisting of one descriptive header and 86 census tracts).
- **Median household income** — 2024 ACS 5-Year Estimates, table B19013. Source: data.census.gov. License: U.S. government work. Accessed 2026-09-21. 87 rows (one descriptive header row plus 86 census tracts).
- **Census tract boundaries** — 2024 TIGER/Line Shapefiles. Source: census.gov TIGER/Line. License: U.S. government work. Accessed 2026-09-21. 85 tracts in Albany County, New York.

## Methods

I will compare median gross rent and median household income across census tracts in Albany. I will calculate a housing affordability measure by comparing annual rent to annual household income. Then, I will join the results to the census tract boundaries and create a map to show where housing costs are higher or lower relative to income.

This project uses median household income for all households (ACS table B19013), not renter households specifically, because the Census Bureau's standard tract-level tables do not separate the two. A classmate raised this as a concern during the proposal presentation: if renters earn less than homeowners within the same tract, using the all-household median could understate how much rent actually burdens renters. This is a real limitation of the available data, and the affordability measure in this project should be read as comparing rent to overall tract income, not specifically to renter income.

### Spatial Pitfalls

Census tracts do not represent individual households. Housing costs and income can vary within the same census tract. Also, census tracts have different population sizes. I will keep these limitations in mind when interpreting the map and will describe the results as area-level patterns rather than conditions for individual households.

## Expected Results

I expect housing affordability to vary across census tracts in Albany. Some areas may have higher housing costs relative to household income, while other areas may be more affordable. The final map will help show these differences across Albany.

## Next Steps

The next step is to clean and combine the ACS data with the census tract boundaries. I will calculate housing affordability for each census tract and create a map to compare different areas in Albany. After creating the map, I will review the results and explain the main patterns.

## IRB

This project uses publicly available data from the U.S. Census Bureau and does not involve human subjects. Therefore, IRB approval is not required.
